newsitem.title: UK: Unionist Paisley demands change in N.Irish talks.
newsitem.headline: Unionist Paisley demands change in N.Irish talks.

text.p: Ian Paisley, leader of Northern Ireland's pro-British Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), on Thursday demanded a change in the format of planned all-party talks to prevent unionists being obliged to sit down with allies of the IRA.
Without changes the talks were "dead in the water", he said.

Paisley, whose party is the second largest Protestant grouping in Northern Ireland, made the call at talks in London with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam who is struggling to get all the parties together for talks on the future of the province.
The DUP leader confirmed his party would boycott peace talks if the Irish Republican Army's political wing Sinn Fein, who want Northern Ireland to be part of the Republic, was invited to them.

His talks with Mowlam came a day after she met Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams. His party was invited to the talks after the IRA declared a new ceasefire on July 20 after 28 years of battle to end British rule in the province.
Paisley presented Mowlam with his party's proposals for restructuring of the talks, which he said "would not force any member to sit down with the IRA".
He told journalists afterwards that if the British government did not accept changes to the format, the talks would founder for lack of unionist support.
"If they don't change the basis of it, then they are only digging their own grave," Paisley said.
Mowlam said she was still hopeful that talks in which all Northern Ireland parties would participate could get under way on September 15.
"I am hopeful that in the weeks ahead we can discuss some mechanisms that we can achieve to keep everybody in the talks process," she said.

The largest Northern Ireland party, the Ulster Unionists, is still considering whether to join in the September talks. It is demanding a clear link between their progress and a willingness by the IRA to give up huge caches of arms and explosives.
